narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

narration: The Beat That Conquered the World
This is makossa. 20th century.

Title card: makossa · Cameroon · 20th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Makossa originated in Douala in the 1950s, evolving from the traditional 'kossa' dance.
It was shaped by the confluence of local rhythms like ambasse bey and assiko with international genres such as highlife, merengue, and Congolese rumba.
on_screen: Map: Cameroon · Africa
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a social dance to stimulate energy and joy, it became a symbol of cultural sovereignty during the independence era.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music features a strong electric bass, prominent brass sections, guitars, and bottle percussion.
It is typically in 4/4 time with a tempo of 130-170 BPM.
Listen for the electric bass, guitar, brass section, bottle (idiophone).
The pulse is 4/4 at about 150 beats a minute.
A driving, bass-heavy sound characterized by tight brass arrangements, syncopated guitar picking, and the rhythmic use of a bottle as percussion.

music_brief.purpose: copyright-free soundtrack with the same DNA as the tradition's music — an original creation, not a reproduction
music_brief.rhythm_pattern: Syncopated and jerky, influenced by assiko and rumba
music_brief.vocal_style: Lead vocalist with a choir of backup singers
music_brief.sound_description: A driving, bass-heavy sound characterized by tight brass arrangements, syncopated guitar picking, and the rhythmic use of a bottle as percussion.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of makossa (Cameroon). Meter 4/4. Tempo about 150 bpm. Rhythm pattern: Syncopated and jerky, influenced by assiko and rumba. Instruments: electric bass, guitar, brass section, bottle (idiophone), drum set, synthesizers. Vocal style: Lead vocalist with a choir of backup singers. Form: Verse-chorus with instrumental breaks (sebene). Mood: energetic, frenzied, syncopated, joyful. It should sound like this: A driving, bass-heavy sound characterized by tight brass arrangements, syncopated guitar picking, and the rhythmic use of a bottle as percussion. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
